  • CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938.
  • CISA urges organizations to take the following actions:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that purpose CISA strongly urges organizations to immediately patch the recently disclosed Oracle Java vulnerability CVE-2026-114938. This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as “Java4Shell,” affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK). Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution. Actions to take CISA urges organizations to take the following actions: Identify affected Java installations. Review your software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party applications or included in container images and appliances. Note: JDKs and Java runtimes may not appear as separate entries in software inventories. Apply relevant Java and vendor patches as soon as they are available, prioritizing internet-facing systems. If immediate patching is not feasible, implement temporary compensating controls, such as restricting and validating Base64 input at the application boundary, enforcing input-size limits, and limiting unauthenticated access. Review Oracle’s security advisory for guidance on patching and affected products and versions. Monitor for indicators of suspicious activity, including rogue runtimes, unexpected JVM crashes, and suspicious Java processes. Resources CISA urges network defenders to review the following resource and apply necessary updates: Vendor Guidance Oracle’s Security Advisory: Critical Security Patch Patch – November 2026 Disclaimer The information in this report is being provided “as is” for informational purposes only. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (926 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles.
  • The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window.
  • Sources indicate that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:.

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

Sources indicate that we recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:.

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

According to recent reports, daisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

In a recent development, we built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

We selected tasks using three criteria:.

In a recent development, radixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

According to recent reports, 2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Sources indicate that every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

Recent findings suggest that the service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Industry observers note that cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

According to recent reports, we thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

Sources indicate that advancements in model post-training are interesting because they can improve how efficiently models handle specialized tasks and complex instructions. For businesses building AI-powered applications, selecting the right model is also an important cost consideration. A larger model is not always necessary for every task, and using appropriately sized models can help balance performance, latency, and API expenses. I've been exploring how model selection and resource optimization influence the overall cost of AI agent systems. This guide shares practical approaches to optimizing AI agent costs: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/resources/blog/ai-agent-cost-optimization.

Industry News: Three-Dimensional Wake Reconstruction and Cross-Scale Transfer for Floating Offshore Wind Turbines via Physics-Informed Fourier Neural Operators

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (242 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31789v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Coupled surge-pitch motions drive unsteady vortex interactions and dynamic wake meandering behind floating offshore wind turbines, complicating three-dimensional wake reconstruction from limited measurements and transfer across turbine scales. Large-eddy simulations coupled with an actuator line model generate fixed and surge-pitch wakes at motion-based Strouhal numbers $St=fD/U_\infty$ of 0.2-0.6 (where $f$, $D$, and $U_\infty$ are the motion frequency, rotor diameter, and inflow velocity) for the National Renewable Energy Laboratory 5 MW ($D=126$ m) and International Energy Agency 22 MW ($D=284$ m) turbines. A physics-informed Fourier neural operator framework combines four-dimensional spectral convolutions with incompressible continuity and rotor-forced momentum-residual regularization to reconstruct three-dimensional unsteady wakes from two observation planes. Trained on the 5 MW fixed and $St=0.2$-$0.5$ cases, the framework recovers near-wake double-peak deficits, motion-driven wake expansion, and coherent vortices through $St=0.6$ (mean wake-center and half-width errors within 1.3% and 1.0% of $D$), while 10% planar sampling preserves near-dense accuracy (relative $L_2$ error 0.0689 versus 0.0684). Applying transfer learning from the 5 MW to the 22 MW turbine lowers the three-dimensional streamwise-velocity error at $St=0.6$ by 36% relative to zero-shot inference (0.1066 to 0.0682), halves scratch-training error with one fixed case (0.0835 versus 0.1693), and restores wake-center tracking and motion-locked harmonics ($St$-$3St$). Large-scale motion-induced dynamics transfer cleanly across turbine scales, whereas fine-scale vortex breakdown remains damped. The framework indicates potential for three-dimensional wake reconstruction and downstream-inflow assessment in floating wind farms.

It has been revealed that view CSAF Summary .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API contains multiple vulnerabilities that could allow an attacker to obtain sensitive information or write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory. Siemens has released a newly introduced version for .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API and recommends to patch to the latest version. The following versions of Siemens .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API are affected: .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API vers:intdot/<3.3.61, vers:intdot/<3.3.62 (CVE-2026-85114, CVE-2026-85115) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 7.5 Siemens .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API 2 Vulnerabilities Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal'), Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Critical Manufacturing Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Firm Headquarters Location: Germany Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-85114 Affected applications do not properly validate filenames received from remote servers during ticket downloads. This could allow an attacker who can manipulate the ticket response to write arbitrary files outside the intended download directory and, when overwriting is enabled, replace existing files accessible to the application. Read More 1 Affected Product .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.61 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to V3.3.61 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 7.5 HIGH CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:N View CVE Details CVE-2026-85115 Affected applications do not properly redact PLC restore passwords from HTTP error exception messages. This could allow an attacker with access to logs or other diagnostic output to obtain the plaintext restore password and potentially perform unauthorized operations on the PLC. Read More 2 Affected Products .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.61 Product Status: known_affected Remediations .NET Client Library for SIMATIC S7 Webserver API < V3.3.62 Product Status: known_affected Remediations Vendor fixUpdate to V3.3.62 or later version Additional Metrics Relevant CWE: CWE-209 Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information CVSS Version Base Score Base Severity Vector String 3.1 5.5 MEDIUM CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N View CVE Details Acknowledgments Siemens ProductCERT reported these vulnerabilities to CISA. General Recommendations As a general security measure, Siemens strongly recommends to protect network access to devices with appropriate mechanisms. In order to operate the devices in a protected IT environment, Siemens recommends to configure the environment according to Siemens' operational guidelines for Industrial Security (Download: https://www.siemens.com/cert/operational-guidelines-industrial-security), and to follow the recommendations in the product manuals. Additional information on Industrial Security by Siemens can be found at: https://www.siemens.com/industrialsecurity Additional Resources For further inquiries on security vulnerabilities in Siemens products and solutions, please contact the Siemens ProductCERT: https://www.siemens.com/cert/advisories Terms of Use The use of Siemens Security Advisories is subject to the terms and conditions listed on: https://www.siemens.com/productcert/terms-of-use. Recommended Practices CISA recommends owners take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. Recommended Practices CISA recommends users take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. VISOR: A Vision-Language Selector for Multimodal Time-Series Forecasting

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (210 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31780v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent time-series foundation models (TSFMs) forecast a distribution over futures, and multimodal time-series (TS) forecasting further exploits other modalities to improve forecasting accuracy. However, existing works have two limitations: 1) TSFMs reduce the predictive distribution to its median or mean, flattening diverse futures into a calm line, and 2) multimodal TS forecasting models incorporate text into the forecaster through TS-language alignment, which is substantially weaker than vision-language alignment. To address these limitations, we propose the VIsion-language SelectOR (VISOR), a multimodal TS forecasting framework that selects one plausible future instead of averaging across candidates, leveraging the alignment capabilities of vision-language models (VLMs) to select the most suitable candidate based on textual information. VISOR consists of two components: 1) a text-free stochastic predictor that samples diverse candidate futures, and 2) a VLM selector that reads the candidates as a single chart image and selects one based on the text. To avoid overly calm forecasting paths, we train the selector with a shape-aware target that evaluates each candidate based on both point-wise error and path shape. Across three benchmarks covering ten datasets, VISOR achieves the best average ranking in both point and volatility errors compared with TSFMs and multimodal TS forecasting models. Code: https://github.com/seunghan96/VISOR.

Industry News: Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3834 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.
  • Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing.
  • In a recent development, take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Industry observers note that models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

In a recent development, take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

It has been revealed that our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

Recent findings suggest that we leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:.

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

In a recent development, for this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:.

Sources indicate that we used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:.

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:.

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

It has been revealed that A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example indicates how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

According to recent reports, the pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

According to recent reports, each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:.

The figure below demonstrates how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

It has been revealed that harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which revealed that 0.1 worked best).

Recent findings suggest that we performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then indicated signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:.

Industry observers note that before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

Recent findings suggest that we also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

In a recent development, we concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:.

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own patch. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):.

It has been revealed that "Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Recent findings suggest that despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

In a recent development, use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

In a recent development, the ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

In a recent development, during training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets fresh tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

According to recent reports, on the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi automatically applies context compaction, while OpenCode and Hermes don't, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Industry observers note that every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

In a recent development, all three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

In a recent development, under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

According to recent reports, this question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

Industry observers note that this phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

In a recent development, we also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

According to recent reports, thanks for such a nice and detailed blog on it. Can you also share, how many iterations did this take, and roughly how long end to end? What would be the minimum GPU requirements to train. Also curious how you think the adapter holds up when the harness changes.

Industry observers note that nice article guys!For adapters merging, one cool idea would be to do MOPD where the student is Qwen3.8-27B (the original one) and teachers are the RL lora adapted one. The random selection of the harness selects the teacher.

Recent findings suggest that view CSAF Summary Successful exploitation of these vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to retrieve sensitive system information, access application data without authorization, recover stored credentials, or intercept and manipulate network communications. The following versions of Dorsett Controls InfoScan are affected: InfoScan <=1.45.0 (CVE-2026-117659, CVE-2026-120157, CVE-2026-120255, CVE-2026-120260, CVE-2026-120271, CVE-2026-120298) CVSS Vendor Equipment v3 8.1 Dorsett Controls InfoScan 5 Vulnerabilities Improper Certificate Validation, Exposure of Sensitive System Information to an Unauthorized Control Sphere, Use of Hard-coded Cryptographic Key, Missing Authentication for Critical Function, Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information Background Critical Infrastructure Sectors: Water and Wastewater Systems Countries/Areas Deployed: Worldwide Tech giant Headquarters Location: United States Vulnerabilities Expand All + CVE-2026-117659 The InfoScan Electron desktop client improperly handles TLS certificate errors by accepting certificates without validating their trustworthiness. The client also configures Electron with nodeIntegration enabled, contextIsolation disabled, and webSecurity disabled. These settings weaken the client’s security boundaries. An attacker who is able to intercept or manipulate network communications may be able to present an untrusted certificate without the application rejecting the connection. Once the System Maintenance application is open, select Check for Updates, and click the Install Now button in the Ready To Install section. If you are an offline customer (InfoScan has no internet access), you will need to download the update from the Dorsett Controls Customer Portal by selecting the InfoScan Update tile, downloading the update, and following the instructions listed on the portal. Recommended Practices CISA recommends owners take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities. Minimize network exposure for all control system devices and/or systems, ensuring they are not accessible from the internet. Locate control system networks and remote devices behind firewalls and isolating them from business networks. When remote access is required, use more secure methods, such as Virtual Private Networks (VPNs), recognizing VPNs may have vulnerabilities and should be updated to the most current version available. Also recognize VPN is only as secure as the connected devices. CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures. CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies. CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets. Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies. Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents. CISA also recommends users take the following measures to protect themselves from social engineering attacks: Do not click web links or open attachments in unsolicited email messages. Refer to Recognizing and Avoiding Email Scams for more information on avoiding email scams. Refer to Avoiding Social Engineering and Phishing Attacks for more information on social engineering attacks. No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time. CISA recommends customers take defensive measures to minimize the risk of exploitation of these vulnerabilities.

CISA reminds organizations to perform proper impact analysis and risk assessment prior to deploying defensive measures.

CISA also provides a section for control systems security recommended practices on the ICS webpage on cisa.gov/ics. Several CISA products detailing cyber defense best practices are available for reading and download, including Improving Industrial Control Systems Cybersecurity with Defense-in-Depth Strategies.

CISA encourages organizations to implement recommended cybersecurity strategies for proactive defense of ICS assets.

Additional mitigation guidance and recommended practices are publicly available on the ICS webpage at cisa.gov/ics in the technical information paper, ICS-TIP-12-146-01B--Targeted Cyber Intrusion Detection and Mitigation Strategies.

Organizations observing suspected malicious activity should follow established internal procedures and report findings to CISA for tracking and correlation against other incidents.

No known public exploitation specifically targeting these vulnerabilities has been reported to CISA at this time.

#10801. SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (262 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

SPARQL-Planned Single-Hop Traversal over a Live Knowledge Graph for Multi-Hop Question Answering

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (262 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31771v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Semantic retrieval struggles with multi-hop question answering on both recall and precision: gold passages are buried among distractors that degrade the reader's answer, and retrieving them requires reasoning over the query rather than matching it. GraphRAG techniques expand semantic retrieval by connecting passages to graph nodes and performing one or more hops of expansion after initial retrieval. This improves recall, but multi-hop expansion becomes expensive and brings additional noise into the retrieved set. We break this tradeoff by \emph{interleaving} dense retrieval with knowledge-graph traversal for complex multi-hop questions. Dense retrieval locates the first relevant regions of the search space at good recall, while traversal of a pre-existing external KG (Wikidata) restores precision and improves recall by confirming retrieved passages against a reasoning path through the KG. To keep traversal both question-adaptive and reliable, we have an LLM plan it as code generation task for graph traversal in SPARQL format but \emph{parse rather than execute} the query. On full 1{,}000-question splits under a shared corpus and reader, and with a single configuration applied identically to every dataset, we reach \textbf{62.5 / 75.1} EM/F1 on HotpotQA, \textbf{73.5 / 81.0} on 2WikiMultiHopQA, and \textbf{37.1 / 50.0} on MuSiQue, ahead of reproduced HippoRAG2, T\textsuperscript{2}RAG, and IRCoT on all three benchmarks. A second, token-matched setting stays ahead of T\textsuperscript{2}RAG on HotpotQA and 2Wiki while spending roughly its per-query budget. Executing the generated SPARQL instead of parsing it costs up to 11.4 EM, mostly because raw queries return empty results, not because of syntax errors.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

View CSAF Summary On October 21, 2026, the Node.js project released security updates addressing a critical vulnerability in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js, commonly referred to as "Node2Shell" (tracked as CVE-2026-111497). The vulnerability is an out-of-bounds write that could allow a remote attacker to cause memory corruption and potentially execute arbitrary code. This advisory covers the status of impact of various Siemens software products. Please also have a look on following Software Field Bulletins: Teamcenter: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869204 Polarion: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869197 Manufacturing Operations Center (Opcenter) and Process Preparation X: https://support.sw.siemens.com/en-US/knowledge-base/PL8869211 Siemens is preparing fixes and recommends specific mitigations for products where fixes are not or not yet available. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.
  • AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work.
  • It has been revealed that AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn one person’s process into your team’s process, get more done in the Quick web app, and get more complete answers from agents working together.

AWS Quick is the AI workspace built only for work. Today, we are releasing updates that help your team get more of its everyday work done:.

It has been revealed that AI assistants make individuals faster, but the gains often stay with one person. The way one analyst builds the monthly report rarely becomes the way the team builds it, and work waits until someone is back at their desk. This release helps your team turn what one person knows into a process everyone can rely on, and keeps work moving when you step away.

Industry observers note that AWS Quick Flows already helps teams automate and standardize business processes so people can focus on their most notable work. Now you can build, run, and refine flows entirely in chat. And your flows can take on more of your tough work, whether you start it from the web, desktop, or mobile app.

For example, here is how flows could support a finance team. Maya is a financial planning and analysis manager at a retailer. Each month, she prepares a report for her VP of Finance that explains changes to costs and margins. For each region, she pulls last month’s results, compares them to the initiative in a spreadsheet, writes commentary on the biggest changes, and sends the report. The process lives in her memory and a personal checklist. When she is out, a teammate has to rebuild the report from scratch, and it looks different every time.

With Quick, Maya can standardize the process, automate it, and make it available to her team. She describes her process in chat, the way she would explain it to a new employee. Quick builds the flow from her description and she tests and refines it in the same conversation. A diagram beside the chat demonstrates each step, so she can confirm it matches how she works.

In a recent development, figure 1: Maya describes her monthly report in chat, and Quick builds the flow with a diagram beside it. Both views, enlarged here for visibility, appear side by side in the same Quick window.

A flow can now bring together agents, skills, tools, and data, and handle longer processes with more data. Fixed calculations and checks keep the results consistent, agents draft and analyze, and Maya decides what goes in the final report. On each run, her flow:.

Industry observers note that maya publishes the flow for her team. At the next month-end, she is at a planning meeting, so Jordan, an analyst on her team, runs it from chat in the Quick desktop app. There, the flow can use a spreadsheet of regional adjustments saved on his computer. Before the report goes out, Jordan reviews the draft, including why each region was flagged, asks for a few changes in chat, and approves it for the VP of Finance. When Priya joins the team, she runs the same flow at her first month-end, and the report is built the same way.

While this is a fictional example, real customers tell us they’re automating complex business processes to make them more consistent and repeatable. This gives their people back valuable time to focus on more strategic work. Take Pomelo, a Latin American fintech provider powering card issuance, processing, and payment operations for customers:.

“At Pomelo, AWS Quick changed who gets to build solutions. Before, every analysis or automation depended on the data team. Today, people across every area explore information, make decisions, and build their own agents and flows within a unified, governed environment. Without growing our team, nearly four times as many people now work with data each month, so our data team can focus on its most complex, high-impact work. A single use case already saves us 80 hours of work per month. But the real transformation isn’t the hours we save. Quick is transforming our data and innovation culture: we’ve gone from a few people building solutions for many to an organization where everyone can create, experiment, and change the way they work. And we’re just getting started.”.

— Rodrigo Marini, Head of Data, Pomelo Fintech Services S.A.S.

Sources indicate that if you already use Quick in your browser, the updated web app puts the items that need your attention on the home screen as soon as you sign in. A reorganized left navigation brings agents, flows, skills, knowledge, and connectors together under Customize. It includes the agents and skills you built on desktop and ones others have shared with you. Your existing dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before, and you do not need to turn anything on.

Figure 2: The feed brings the morning’s email and messages that need a reply into one view.

Industry observers note that some requests need the knowledge of more than one specialized agent. With multi-agent orchestration, the agent you ask can bring in several specialized agents at once, each working on the part it knows best. The agent then combines their work into one response. Each agent keeps its own instructions, knowledge, and context, so the people who know that work best can build and maintain it.

It has been revealed that for example, you might ask why shipping costs rose in one region. Your agent can bring in a forecasting agent built on your team’s planning data and a procurement agent built on the procurement team’s vendor contracts. You get one response that reveals what each agent contributed, and you decide what to do with it.

It has been revealed that work lives in many systems. This release adds new connectors so Quick can pull from the analytics and tools your team uses every day. Connect once, then ask in natural language.

Industry observers note that meta ads. Create, manage, and analyze Meta ad campaigns in natural language through a connector to Meta’s ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Quick combines Meta ad data with your first-party and third-party sources, and asks for your permission before it creates a campaign, changes a budget, or takes any other write action in an ad account. Try Quick free for 3 months and invite up to 10 teammates at no cost.

Industry observers note that amplitude. Ask about product usage, customer behavior, and conversion in natural language. Quick connects to Amplitude through its MCP server, so product and marketing teams can pull behavioral insights into the dashboards, documents, and workflows they build in Quick.

Connectors respect your existing permissions. Quick only shows each person what they already have access to. Quick asks before it takes any write action. Administrators choose which connectors teams can add.

Whether you build a monthly report, run one your manager built, or set up Quick for your organization, Quick works the way you do. Your data stays in your environment and does not train anyone else’s models. You bring the judgment, and Quick gives your team the capacity to match its goals.

These features are available today in all Regions where AWS Quick is available.

Recent findings suggest that to try what’s new, sign in to Quick or download Quick and get started in minutes. To learn about enterprise pricing aims, talk to your AWS account team.

#10793. Latest Update: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (285 w)

Latest Update: DELTA: Diagnosing Exploration Lineages via Twin-path Alignment - What Can Contrasting Design Paths Reveal About Microarchitectural Behavior?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (285 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31767v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Architects have two mature instruments for performance work. Top-Down analysis tells them where a design loses its pipeline slots, and design-space exploration (DSE) tells them which configuration scores best. Neither explains why a search stops improving: why a backend-bound design rejects a prefetcher that the bottleneck label recommends, or why a capacity increase that helped in one configuration hurts in the next. This paper argues that the evidence needed to answer such questions is already produced during exploration and then discarded. Every parent-child edge in an exploration tree is a controlled intervention: one knob changes, the rest of the design is held fixed, and a cycle-level simulator measures the outcome. When the same edit helps under one parent and hurts under another, aligning the two parents localizes the interaction that decides its sign. We present DELTA, a simulator-grounded root-cause analysis tool that builds a Design Memory of such interventions during exploration and lets an architect query it afterwards. Each record stores the full parent configuration, the single applied edit, the measured and predicted IPC, a Top-Down breakdown from StallLens, our gem5 implementation of Top-Down, and its lineage. Unlike evolutionary LLM search, which keeps only high-scoring programs, DELTA keeps failed edges as evidence. The same memory also makes exploration efficient: on four SPEC CPU2017 workloads, the full system raises IPC by 55.5% in 22 simulated designs for $1.56 of model cost, predicts the IPC of its own proposals to within 3.3%, and keeps improving after a bottleneck-guided search stalls. A root-cause query over the recorded history led us to a usefulness-throttled variant of the Best-Offset prefetcher that improves IPC by 1.37% over the original in matched configurations.

Welcome Inkling 2 Mini, Cutting-edge Performance for your Local Setup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2448 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model.
  • It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups.
  • We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TLDR; Inkling 2 Mini is a new looped transformer model. It’s a multimodal Mixture-of-Experts with ~26B physical total and 3B active parameters per token. It uses a neat trick to increase capacity: some layers are visited in a loop that repeats three times, which makes it work like it had more parameters. It supports a 1M-token context size, accepts images and text inputs. Thinking Machines Lab ships the model in a mixed-precision format, with NVFP4 and MXFP8 expert weights. A DSpark drafter is also included for additional speed-up at a small memory cost.

It has been revealed that inkling 2 Mini is much, much smaller than Inkling 2 Small, and is designed for local AI setups. We think this is a refreshingly upcoming great local model. In our vibe tests, it's at least comparable with Qwen 3.8 27B. More validation is needed, but we are super excited about this release!

We ship transformers, llama.cpp, and MLX support. SGLang also provides day-zero inference support for production deployments on datacenter hardware.

This post goes through what makes Inkling Mini different, some of our vibe tests, and how you can use it with your setup.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 24 decoder layers, but the 12 middle layers run three times in a loop. Therefore, the model acts as if it had 48 (6+ 3*12 + 6) logical layers with just 24 physical ones.

It has been revealed that similar to Inkling 2 Small, Inkling 2 Mini executes 48 layer visits per token. The hidden size is 2,304 instead of 4,608. At each layer visit, both variants route the token to 8 experts, but Mini selects them from among 128 experts per layer, while Small selects from 384.The decoder runs layers 0–5 once, layers 6–17 three times, and layers 18–23 once. All three passes through layers 6–17 reuse the same weights.

Architectures such as Nanbeige have explored looping before. But Inkling 2 Mini explores an interesting approach. Every pass through the looped core (layers 6–17) starts from the same inputs which is the output of the first six layers. Information moves between passes through cross-pass messages. Each looped layer reads a message from the previous pass's outputs with its own learned query (one message for its query, key, value and MLP inputs). A small gating controller then looks at both the layer's current input and the message. It decides how much of the current input to forget and how much of the message to add. Each pass therefore refines what the previous one computed.

Industry observers note that text decoder width is 2,304, and the intermediate width of each expert is 1,152. Reusing core weights reduces the number of distinct layers the checkpoint stores. The model still executes all 48 visits, and each visit keeps its own KV and short-convolution state.

In a recent development, in addition to the flagship Inkling 2 Mini model, a research artifact has also been released. It shares the same architecture, but this variant was trained to accept a variable number of passes through the loop 🤯. Setting 1 or 2 passes instead of 3 will make inference run a lot faster, but generations may be of slightly lower quality. We tested this variant, and it works, but we haven’t evaluated it in depth.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is state-of-the-art in its class in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5 (AAv5), as well as across many benchmarks in various categories. Compared with Gemma 4 31B, Muse Glimmer, Qwen3.8-27B, and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, Inkling 2 Mini leads in 32 benchmarks out of 48. These cover coding and autoresearch, agentic search and tool use for knowledge work, vision interpretation and creation, reasoning and knowledge, and safety and alignment. See the Inkling 2 Mini model card for the full list of benchmarks and scores.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini is a great local coding companion. It leads in FrontierCode v2.0, ties with Qwen3.8-27B on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and trails Qwen on AutomationBench-AA v1.0.6. You can check out a few of our highlights below for coding and knowledge work. Note that AA Briefcase is in ELO rating, higher is better.

In this section, you can find how to use Inkling 2 Mini in transformers, llama.cpp, MLX, and SGLang.

We provide support for both Inkling 2 Mini (fixed loop) and the TML-d24-varloop-research (variable loop) research variant.

You can use the AutoModelForMultimodalLM class.

To set the number of loops in the research checkpoint, you can modify the loop_num_passes in text_config as follows. The example below uses two loops.

For an image prompt, replace messages in either example with the list below and infer as usual.

Pass reasoning_effort="medium" to processor.apply_chat_template(...) to set the effort for a request. The chat template adds the numeric value to the prompt as a system message. The default is high (0.9).

Available levels are none (0.0), minimal (0.1), low (0.2), medium (0.7), high (0.9; default), xhigh (0.99), and max (0.99). You can also pass a number from 0.0 to 0.99, such as reasoning_effort=0.35.

Let’s get our model to call some tools.

It has been revealed that in this example we ask our model about the current temperature at a given location. With the prompt, we also provide the tool (get_current_temperature) to do it. The model asks for a tool call, we call the tool on its behalf and then add the output to the next instruction set. It uses the output of the tool and provides us with the final result.

If you want to know more about tool calling, we recommend going to our official docs.

Sources indicate that inkling 2 Mini comes with Day 0 support inside SGLang. You can install the latest version of SGLang and execute the following to get the server up and running. One prerequisite to take care of is to run it on SM103.

After the server is up you should be able to request the APIs like so.

One can also enable multimodality by setting --enable-multimodal.

SGLang can use a three-layer DSpark draft to propose tokens for the target model to verify. The draft reads the inputs to decoder visits 5, 23, and 41, plus the final normalized state at index 48. With the draft weights present, add --speculative-algorithm DSPARK --context-length 131072 to the server command.

We benchmarked the models with and without speculative decoding, and measured generation speed on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU where every request has a 1,024-token prompt and generates exactly 1,024 tokens and concurrency of 1, 4, 16 and 64.

We upstreamed MLX support to the mlx-lm project, including multimodal image and text inputs, and shared quants through the mlx-community organization.

We have given Inkling 2 Mini a shot in many fun tasks, check them out in this section.

The same prompt produced two sunset flythroughs over procedural mountains and reflective water, each rendered with a single WebGL fragment shader.

Build the most impressive original real-time scene you can: a slow, cinematic camera flight over procedural mountains, through volumetric clouds and low over water with reflections, all lit by a sunset. Deliver it as a single self-contained index.html in the current directory that renders everything in one full-screen WebGL fragment shader, purely from code (no textures, images, fonts, libraries, external files or network requests of any kind). It must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080, aiming for 60 fps on a desktop GPU, with an automatic resolution-scale fallback that lowers the internal render resolution when the frame rate drops, and the flight must keep going indefinitely without glitches. To check your work, run node shot.cjs index.html shot.png 6 (the third argument is how many seconds to wait; a comma list such as 3,12,25 saves one screenshot per time, and an optional fourth argument sets the size, default 1280x720): it renders the page in headless Chrome, saves the screenshot(s), and prints the WebGL renderer, a rough frame rate and any console errors; then look at the images. The headless renderer on this machine may be software-only, so its frame rate can be far below what a real desktop GPU achieves and is not the target. Decide for yourself when the result is finished, then reply with a short description of what you built.

Vincent van Gogh, The Starry Night (1889).

According to recent reports, we gave Inkling 2 Mini a reference image of Van Gogh’s painting and a screenshot helper in the Pi coding harness. Inkling wrote a self-contained HTML page with a single WebGL2 fragment shader. The shader draws the scene from code without loading the reference image or any other assets. It uses time to animate the swirling sky, the glow of the stars, the swaying cypress, and the flicker of the village windows.

Inkling rendered and reviewed its work over 24 rounds of screenshot checks. We recorded the final animation frame by frame at 1080p and 60 fps on an Apple M4 Max.

In this folder, starry-night.jpg is Vincent van Gogh's The Starry Night (1889, public domain). Recreate it as a living painting: a single self-contained index.html (all code inline, no external files, libraries or network requests) that fills the browser window and runs smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Everything must be generated procedurally in code, for example with WebGL shaders; the page must not load, embed or sample starry-night.jpg or any other image. Stay faithful to the painting's composition and palette (the great spiral and swirling currents of the sky, the haloed stars, the glowing crescent moon, the dark flame-like cypress on the left, the rolling hills, and the village with its church spire), rendered in Van Gogh's thick, directional brushstrokes, and bring it to life: the sky's swirls flow, the stars and moon pulse with light, the cypress sways, and the village windows glow and flicker. Aim for the most impressive result you can make. A helper is provided: run node shot.js --help to see how to screenshot index.html at several moments; look at the screenshots next to the reference and keep improving until you are satisfied, then reply with a short summary of what you made.

It has been revealed that we gave Inkling 2 Mini a photo of a hand-drawn Trip Split wireframe and a one-paragraph prompt in the Pi coding harness. Inkling used the sketch’s labels, sample expenses, and handwritten notes to build the expense list, add-expense form, and balances view in a single HTML file with vanilla CSS and JavaScript. The app updates totals and balances when expenses change, suggests payments to settle the trip, and saves data in the browser’s localStorage so it survives a reload.

We ran three independent Inkling attempts and used Playwright to click through each build, checking screenshots where visual judgment was needed. The first attempt, shown here, passed all 13 checks. Adding the sketch’s $90 dinner raised the total from $405 to $495 and recalculated what each person owed.

The photo sketch.jpg in this folder is a product designer's hand-drawn wireframe of a small app. Build that app for real, as the most impressive, original, production-quality version you can make: a single self-contained index.html in this folder using vanilla HTML, CSS and JavaScript only (no frameworks, CDNs, external files or network requests; localStorage is fine), which must run smoothly in desktop Chrome at 1920x1080. Treat everything on the paper as the spec: every screen, label, button and number, the example data, and each red note describe behaviour that must actually work, while the visual design, typography and motion are yours to make beautiful. Look at the sketch carefully with your vision, and use your vision again to check your own work: node shot.cjs --help explains a provided helper that screenshots index.html in headless Chrome at any window size after clicks or other JavaScript steps (Playwright is also installed if you prefer your own scripts), and you can look at any screenshot with the read tool. Click through every feature, compare each screen against the sketch, and keep improving until you are fully satisfied; then reply with a short summary of what you built.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, CISA has added four new vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, based on evidence of active exploitation. CVE-2024-10441 Synology DiskStation Manager (DSM) Improper Encoding or Escaping of Output Vulnerability CVE-2026-40217 BerriAI LiteLLM Unprotected Alternate Channel Vulnerability CVE-2026-90436 Apache Axis Unsafe Reflection Vulnerability CVE-2026-90817 Vanderbilt University Research Electronic Data Capture (REDCap) Code Injection Vulnerability These types of vulnerabilities are a frequent attack vector for malicious cyber actors and pose significant risks to the federal enterprise. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. BOD 26-04 further establishes basic expectations for when agencies must check whether threat actors compromised the system before the patch was applied. While BOD 26-04 applies only to FCEB agencies, CISA encourages all organizations to adopt risk-based vulnerability management and prioritize remediation of KEV Catalog vulnerabilities. CISA will continue to add vulnerabilities to the catalog that meet the specified criteria. Aware of an exploited vulnerability not currently listed in the KEV Catalog? Submit it for potential addition through CISA’s KEV Nomination Form. Potential KEV additions must have a CVE ID, evidence of exploitation, and clear mitigation guidance.

#10787. RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (184 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (184 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31766v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.

Marketers have never had more data to act on. Take an apparel brand that advertises on Meta technologies: campaign results live in Meta Ads Manager, briefs and creative assets in shared storage, and inventory, customer lifetime value, and in-store purchases in a data lake. Analysts export reports, merge spreadsheets, and rebuild the same deck each week, and the data ages before anyone acts on it. When the team does decide what to change, someone returns to Ads Manager to enhancement campaigns, ad sets, budgets, and audiences by hand. As a result, teams judge campaigns on metrics alone, and the path from insight to action stays slow and manual.

Industry observers note that today, AWS Quick added a Meta ads AI connector. The connector gives Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Meta ads customers can use natural language to create, manage, and analyze campaigns within Quick, while staying connected to the Meta ad management network. Marketers can complete tasks with support from AI, such as pulling insights to understand ads performance, creating product catalogs, and editing existing or creating new campaigns. Quick can also combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to create dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows.

Sources indicate that “Meta ads AI connector through Quick gives our marketing teams one place to go from campaign planning to execution. It lets us act on business insights directly in our ads, without the handoffs and tool switching that slow campaigns down. With fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models in the same workflow, we’ll test more creative ideas and spend more time reaching customers.”.

— Tina Sang, Head of Marketing at fal.ai.

The other builds a dashboard comparing spend, leads, and cost per lead for two ad sets, with recommended tests to run next.
